clue.text: Me, acting uncannily like a great puller of babes?

definitions.text: like a great puller of babes?

indicators.note: something done uncannily is weird and unnatural, so the letters come out in a strange new order

blocks.note: the two words taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A man boasts that his acting makes him irresistible to young women.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma splits the fodder from nothing; ME and ACTING together hold the eight letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A magnet is a great puller in the physical sense, and a magnetic person attracts admirers, so the question mark flags the pun.

clue.text: Blimp broadcasts with fruity thing

blocks.note: to air a programme is to broadcast it
a hip is the fruit of the rose

explanation.surface: Colonel Blimp, the pompous British cartoon officer, sounds off about something rude.
explanation.walkthrough: Blimp suggests the reactionary old cartoon colonel; here it is the balloon.
explanation.definitionFit: A blimp is a non-rigid airship, a gas-filled craft without an internal frame.

clue.text: (& 19dn.) "INSTITUTE BLOKE UP TO NO GOOD WITH ARTIFICIAL HIP AGAINST GIRL'S TOP" — News of the Screws speciality

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means reading the word from bottom to top
the top of a word is its opening letter

blocks.note: a bloke is British slang for a man
I is the abbreviation for institute
NG is the common abbreviation for no good
and means together with
a sham is fake or artificial
hip and in both mean fashionable
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A mock tabloid headline about a scandalous man, the kind the News of the World ran every week.
explanation.walkthrough: The News of the World was a British Sunday tabloid, nicknamed the News of the Screws for its sex scandals. The setter's word order is loose: I and NG together follow the reversed bloke.
explanation.definitionFit: Naming and shaming means publicly identifying wrongdoers to embarrass them, which was the stock in trade of that scandal sheet.

clue.text: Willy's head buried in pert bust — tosser!

indicators.note: the head of a word is its front, so only the first letter is kept
something bust is broken, so the letters need putting back in a new order
something buried in a thing is surrounded by it on all sides

blocks.note: the first letter of the name
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man presses his face into a perky bosom and gets called a wanker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Willy' and 'pert bust' build a ribald picture; tosser is British slang for a contemptible fool.
explanation.definitionFit: A twerp is a silly, contemptible person, and tosser is a ruder British insult for the same kind of idiot.

clue.text: Unoriginal hack's submission on "pussy"

blocks.note: copy is the text a journalist files
pussy is a pet name for a cat

explanation.surface: A tabloid reporter files a smutty story about a cat.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks around 'pussy' invite the rude reading, but it is only the pet name for a family pet. 'On' works in a down clue: the first part sits on top of the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Copycat as an adjective describes something that imitates another, so it lacks originality.

clue.text: As the police's young black victim was South American, Sun editorial much reduced?

definitions.text: As the police's young black victim was

indicators.note: cutting each word down a great deal leaves only its opening letter or two

blocks.note: S is the compass abbreviation for south
US, as in a US citizen, stands for American
the word cut right down to its first letter
the word cut down to its first two letters, the usual short form of editor or editorial

explanation.surface: A grim comment on a police shooting and how little space a tabloid gave it.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain 'sus' was police slang for stopping people on mere suspicion, notoriously used against young black men; a black youth stopped like that had been 'sussed'. The South American victim alludes to the Brazilian Jean Charles de Menezes.
explanation.definitionFit: To be sussed is to be suspected or found out, which is how the police treated their victim in the setter's satirical reading.

clue.text: Members backing 'the old man' and party getting suddenly dropped as a punishment

definitions.text: getting suddenly dropped as a punishment
definitions.note: describes the punishment by its method; the answer is the noun naming it

indicators.note: moving backwards means the word is read from end to start

blocks.note: parts are the members of a whole
the old man is slang for one's father
a do is a party

explanation.surface: Party members turn against their ageing leader, who is suddenly ditched.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Members backing' sounds like supporters of a leader, but backing means reversal.
explanation.definitionFit: Strappado was a torture in which the victim, hoisted by the wrists, was let fall and jerked to a halt.

clue.text: Take off second big girl's blouse

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for second
big girl's blouse is a British insult for a feeble, unmanly man; poof is an offensive slang term in the same vein

explanation.surface: An instruction to remove a second large blouse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take off' suggests undressing and blouse suggests clothing; both mislead, as the answer means a parody.
explanation.definitionFit: A take-off is an imitation that mocks its original, and a spoof is the same kind of humorous parody.

clue.text: Measure energy consumed by tart about to solicit

indicators.note: something consumed is taken inside, so one letter goes within the word
turned about means shifted around, so the combined letters are rearranged

blocks.note: an en is a printer's measure of width
E is the symbol for energy
taken as written

explanation.surface: A prostitute is about to proposition a customer, measuring the energy it takes.
explanation.walkthrough: Tart and solicit together suggest street prostitution; solicit here just means to beg or ask earnestly.
explanation.definitionFit: To entreat is to ask someone earnestly for something, which is one sense of solicit.

clue.text: Formidable old farm worker who'll make you stiff

blocks.note: grim means stern and forbidding
a reaper cut corn by hand, a job machines took over long ago

explanation.surface: A tough old farmhand is said to leave you sore and aching.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stiff' suggests aching muscles or worse, but a stiff is a corpse.
explanation.definitionFit: The Grim Reaper is the personification of death, who turns the living into stiffs, slang for corpses.

clue.text: Curse of Hello's ultimate hat trick

indicators.note: ultimate means final, so only the closing letter of the word is wanted
a trick played on the letters jumbles them into a new order

blocks.note: the final letter of the greeting
taken as written

explanation.surface: A jinx attached to a celebrity magazine's best conjuring act with a hat.
explanation.walkthrough: Hello! is a British celebrity magazine; 'hat trick' looks like the cricket or football feat but splits into fodder and indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: An oath can be a swear word, and a curse is likewise a profane exclamation.

clue.text: Don't get down a bottomless ravine with an erection

indicators.note: without a bottom means the word loses its final letter

blocks.note: a chine is a deep narrow ravine, a word used on the Isle of Wight and in Dorset
something erected stands up

explanation.surface: Advice not to climb down into a gorge, with a smutty twist.
explanation.walkthrough: Chine is a dialect word for a steep-sided coastal ravine, common on the Isle of Wight and in Dorset; the stray 'a' only smooths the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Chin up is an idiom of encouragement telling someone not to be dejected, which is what 'don't get down' urges.

clue.text: Grope out of place: 'e's penetrated

indicators.note: the short word has gone into the middle of the longer phrase
letters that are out of their normal order need rearranging

blocks.note: the two words taken letter for letter
the Cockney 'e, with its dropped H, is just the letter E

explanation.surface: An unwanted grope is out of order, and the man has made a sexual advance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out of place' reads as one disapproving phrase, but 'out' is the anagram signal and 'of place' the fodder, with the E slipped in.
explanation.definitionFit: To cop a feel is slang for touching someone sexually without consent, the same act as groping.

clue.text: Posh uses crap make-up, right?

indicators.note: something crap is badly made, so these letters are botched into a new order

blocks.note: the word taken letter for letter, hyphen dropped
RT is a standard abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A jibe that Posh Spice, Victoria Beckham, wears cheap cosmetics.
explanation.walkthrough: Posh looks like Victoria Beckham's nickname, but it is the definition; 'crap' is the anagram signal, not a verdict.
explanation.definitionFit: Upmarket describes goods or places aimed at wealthy, classy buyers, which is what posh means as an adjective.

clue.text: Aroused in the club

blocks.note: first meaning: woken by a knock on the door, old British usage
second meaning: British slang for pregnant

explanation.walkthrough: 'Aroused in the club' paints a nightclub scene; in the club is also British slang for pregnant.
explanation.definitionFit: Knocked up means both roused from sleep by knocking (British) and, as slang, made pregnant, which matches being in the club.

clue.text: Toff entertained by Paris, topless!

indicators.note: a guest entertained by someone is held within their house, so the word sits inside the following letters

blocks.note: runs from the second letter of the city to the start of the last word

explanation.surface: A posh man enjoys a topless show laid on by the French capital, or by Paris Hilton.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Topless' also neatly hints that the first letter of Paris is dropped. A toff is British slang for an upper-class person.
explanation.definitionFit: Aristo is short for aristocrat, and a toff is a rich, upper-class person, so the two are slang synonyms.

clue.text: He's thin, broken by sex and likely to get a bollocking

indicators.note: a broken thing is in pieces, ready to be put back together differently

blocks.note: the words taken letter for letter
it is a coy word for sex, as in 'doing it'

explanation.surface: A skinny man, worn out by sex, is about to be told off.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in the shit is slang for being in serious trouble, and a bollocking is British slang for a severe telling-off.

clue.text: Di's out getting screwed by a film maker

indicators.note: something screwed is twisted round, so the letters are turned into a new order

blocks.note: the words taken letter for letter, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: A woman called Di has gone out and been seduced by a movie director.
explanation.definitionFit: A film studio is the company that produces movies, so it is literally a maker of films.

clue.text: Fundamentalists' match reported by Boycott

definitions.note: the answer is a plural noun; the possessive 's merely joins the definition to the wordplay

indicators.note: something reported is passed on by word of mouth, so the clue words are judged by their sound

blocks.note: to tally is to match or correspond
a boycott is a ban on dealing with someone

explanation.surface: A cricket match involving extremists, reported by Geoffrey Boycott, the Yorkshire batsman turned commentator.
explanation.walkthrough: Spoken together, tally and ban sound like the Afghan movement; Boycott's capital letter is there to suggest the cricketer.
explanation.definitionFit: The Taliban are an Islamist movement known for strict religious fundamentalism.

clue.text: Like Gordon Brown's outdated tax — misconceived shit

indicators.note: something misconceived is badly formed, so the letters are put together wrongly

blocks.note: scot was a medieval tax, surviving in the phrase scot-free
taken as written

explanation.surface: An insult aimed at a tax policy of Gordon Brown, the former British Chancellor and Prime Minister.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gordon Brown's outdated tax' reads as one phrase; the 's is only a joining word and Brown's tax is a red herring.
explanation.definitionFit: Gordon Brown was born in Glasgow and raised in Kirkcaldy, so anything like him is Scottish.

clue.text: (see 3dn.)
Bad to adopt Kennedy's lead, getting as much as one can drink

definitions.text: as much as one can drink

indicators.note: adopting someone takes them into the family, so the letter goes inside the word
the lead of a word is its front, so only the first letter is kept

blocks.note: sinful means wicked or bad
the opening letter of the surname

explanation.surface: A nod to Charles Kennedy, the Liberal Democrat leader whose drinking problem was public, taking a bad lead.
explanation.walkthrough: K goes in after the first letter of SINFUL.
explanation.definitionFit: A skinful is British slang for enough alcohol to make someone drunk, the most one can hold.

clue.text: Where Olav gets pissed with saki?

indicators.note: someone pissed (British for drunk) staggers about, so the letters reel into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Asking where a Scandinavian called Olav got drunk on Japanese rice wine.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue asks for a place, so 'Where' is a bare but fair definition of a country.
explanation.definitionFit: Slovakia is a central European country, a place that answers the question where.

clue.text: One who makes one cross, being oddly over protective of Tories' leader?

indicators.note: doing something oddly means doing it strangely, so the letters fall into an unexpected order
being protective of something means wrapping around it to shield it
a leader comes first, so only the opening letter is wanted

blocks.note: taken as written
the opening letter of the party name

explanation.surface: Someone who annoys people by being strangely overprotective of the Conservative Party leader.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Makes one cross' suggests annoying someone, but it means marking an X on a ballot paper.
explanation.definitionFit: A voter marks a cross beside a candidate's name on the ballot, so a voter is one who makes a cross.

clue.text: Sound of happy slurp of tongue

indicators.note: the sound of something is how it is heard, so the answer is spoken like the clue words

blocks.note: gay in its old sense of happy and carefree
a slurp with the tongue is a lick

explanation.surface: A noisy happy slurping done with the tongue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tongue' looks like the organ doing the slurping, but it means a language.
explanation.definitionFit: Gaelic is the Celtic language of Scotland and Ireland, and tongue is an old word for a language.

clue.text: Pick up Glaxo's head director

indicators.note: the head of a word is its front, so only the first letter is kept

blocks.note: the first letter of the drug company's name
David Lean, British director of Lawrence of Arabia

explanation.surface: Collecting the boss of the drugs firm Glaxo, or perhaps chatting someone up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Glaxo's head director' reads as one company title; it splits into a first letter and a film director.
explanation.definitionFit: To glean is to gather or collect bit by bit, which is to pick up information or leftovers.

clue.text: Account of some perisher in round money

blocks.note: a round letter shape
a bit is a coin, as in a threepenny bit, an old British coin

explanation.surface: Someone's story about a child, a little perisher, and a round of cash.
explanation.walkthrough: A perisher is British slang for a mischievous child, but here it is read literally as someone who has perished.
explanation.definitionFit: An obit, short for obituary, is a published account of the life of someone who has died.

clue.text: Whirling dervish has behind that produces a through motion

definitions.note: a noun phrase in a relative-clause form: the thing that produces it

indicators.note: a whirling dancer spins round and round, so these letters are spun into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
aft is the nautical word for at the back

explanation.surface: A spinning dervish's backside creates a lavatorial kind of motion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Has behind' sounds like a body part, and 'through motion' plays on a bowel movement; behind just means AFT, placed at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A drive shaft is the rotating rod that carries power through a vehicle, so it produces motion transmitted from one end to the other.

clue.text: Wild hen party, skirts removed to take part in a tabloid sting?

definitions.text: take part in a tabloid sting

indicators.note: the skirts are the outer edges, so the phrase loses its first and last letters
something wild is unruly, so the remaining letters run riot into a new order

blocks.note: a hen party is a British bachelorette party

explanation.surface: A rowdy bachelorette party where the women strip off, all set up by a tabloid newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing the outer letters leaves ENPART before the shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: A tabloid sting lures a target into wrongdoing, so to entrap is exactly to take part in one as the trapper.

clue.text: Member, nuts about stealing

indicators.note: turned about means scattered around, so the letters go into a different order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone in a club or party is crazy about thieving.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nuts about' looks like 'keen on', but 'nuts' belongs with 'Member' as slang for body parts and 'about' alone signals the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: Member is slang for the penis and nuts for the testicles, so together they make up the male sexual organs.
